newsitem.title: USA: Clinton has no plans to call off Carville.
newsitem.headline: Clinton has no plans to call off Carville.

text.p: President Clinton said Tuesday he has no plans to try to stop political adviser James Carville from mounting a campaign against Whitewater independent counsel Kenneth Starr.
Carville, a key adviser in Clinton's 1992 election who maintains strong ties to the White House, has said he plans an all-out campaign to attack Starr as a prosecutor with a Republican bias.
Clinton, during an Oval Office event, said he had no comment on Carville's activities. Asked if he planned to talk to Carville about it, Clinton replied: "No."

Starr is investigating the Whitewater land deal in Arkansas in which Clinton and his wife Hillary invested more than a decade ago. His inquiry has expanded to include the firing of the White House travel office staff in 1993 and the White House's improperly obtaining confidential FBI files on top Republicans.

Much of Washington is waiting to see whether Starr will target Mrs. Clinton or top aides to the president. He has raised expectations of action soon by giving two public speeches laying out the wrongdoing he believes occurred in Whitewater and the travel office affair.
White House spokesman Mike McCurry said Monday that Carville is "certainly someone who speaks for himself and has made it clear he will speak for himself, regardless of what the White House says."

Asked why the president himself did not stop Carville from criticising Starr, McCurry replied: "He's not in a position to dissuade Mr. Carville from pursuing the course that Mr. Carville (has chosen)."
Even Carville's wife, Republican consultant Mary Matalin, has questioned why Clinton does not call off Carville.
"Why is the president letting Carville do this?" the Washington Times quoted her as saying. "Why isn't the press asking him? It's tacit approval."
She suggested that "maybe this is a big scam to get the heat off of Clinton."
